title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership How Candor Keeps the Blue Angels Safe
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay uses the Blue Angels' 'Calling a Safety' post-flight ritual as a model for how leaders can institutionalise psychological safety through deliberate routines that normalise candid self-disclosure. The Blue Angels -- six fighter pilots flying 18 inches apart at 250 knots -- depend on honest communication for literal survival; their solution is a structured debrief in which every pilot self-declares every error using a fixed formula. The ritual makes silence the risky choice: failing to call a safety is the transgression, not making one. The article argues that all teams can benefit from equivalent rituals -- 'Calling a Safety,' 'Holding the Truth Stick,' 'Wearing the Honesty Hat,' 'Using the Cone of Candor' -- that grant structural permission to express what the team most needs to hear. The practical takeaway is a design question for leaders: what ritual can you create to make the risky statements safe to say?
points: - Psychological safety is not a natural team state -- it must be actively designed through rituals and habits that make candid conversation expected, not exceptional. - The Blue Angels invert the normal social calculus: on their team, the risky thing is NOT to call a safety -- silence about a mistake is the transgression, not disclosure of it. - The fixed formula ('take the safety, commit to fixing it, express gratitude') removes social friction from error disclosure by scripting it, making a courageous act into a routine. - Named rituals are more effective than vague encouragement to speak up because they provide a concrete, repeatable social technology for high-risk speech. - Leaders must 'make silence the risky thing' -- a culture shift requiring structural support and deliberate ritual design, not just permission to be candid.
quotes: When they feel psychologically safe, team members believe they can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, challenge ideas, and offer unpopular opinions without being punished, embarrassed, or ignored. Quality decisions, top performance, and continuous learning in teams all depend on this feeling of safety.

This is why the best leaders work hard to normalize candid conversations and make silence the risky thing. One particularly effective way of doing so is to create a ritual that gives people permission to take conversational risk.

With up to six F/A-18 Super Hornets performing flight maneuvers 18 inches apart at 250 knots, few teams in the world depend on trust the way the Blue Angels do. Their lives literally depend on being able to have honest conversations about their performance.
For each error, the pilot announces they are calling a Safety. The pattern is always the same: take the safety, commit to fixing it, and express gratitude for being on the team.

For the Blue Angels, the risky thing is to NOT take a safety. Expressing a contrarian view, a new idea, a critique, or a mistake is not just normal -- it is expected. And everyone is safer, literally and psychologically, as a result.
